analysis.title: "Everything's Fine": Goldman's Pasquariello Says Breadth Isn't So Bad... Then Brings Up The Dot-Com Bubble Twice
key_insights: Pasquariello argues market breadth is not as bad as reported. Most major US indices are up double digits YTD (Dow the exception), all but two S&P sectors are higher on the year, and nearly 2-in-3 S&P names are positive.
Tail counts in the S&P: 123 names are up 25% or more versus 42 down 25% or more, and 53 are up 50% or more versus 8 down 50% or more.

Pasquariello concedes the median S&P stock trades 15% below its 52-week high, the worst reading since the dot-com bubble. ZeroHedge notes he measures from Jan 1, while measured from recent highs about 85% of S&P names are more than 10% below their all-time highs and 17% are more than 50% below.

Goldman's sentiment indicator, described as a positioning meter, has been negative for six straight weeks. Net exposure on Goldman's global prime book is in the 10th percentile of the past year, and the US has been net sold three weeks running.
The S&P broke out last week while a measure of client turnover ranked 49th of the past 52 weeks. Pasquariello expects flows to be net positive from here through the turn.

ZeroHedge counters that the length that exists is concentrated: Mag7 is a record ~22% of Goldman's US prime exposure, and that corner was being unwound on Oct 13 (Kospi down 5.5%, semis on track for a sixth straight loss). Rich Privorotsky said the market got incredibly long one corner and effectively short everything else.
Goldman's 2027 corporate supply and demand note forecasts $600bn of primary issuance including $175bn of IPOs, under 1% of US equity market cap. Buybacks plus M&A should total about $2tr.

Lockup expirations could bring $1.7tr of supply in 2027. Combined with the $600bn of issuance, net US equity supply could rise the most since 2000. ZeroHedge's napkin math puts possible supply at $2.3tr against roughly $2tr of buybacks and M&A.
Nvidia-backed Firmus cut its $5.5 billion IPO by 25% and then pulled it last week.

Pasquariello's directional view is tactically net positive, with technicals improving through October and past the midterms. He calls 2027 a complicated year, citing the supply picture and a broad deceleration of earnings growth.

His short-term plan is to stay short fixed income and stay long NDX, TPX and GSCI. On Oct 13 Treasuries rallied (10Y -4bps to 5.19%) while Nasdaq futures slid, so both legs moved against him before the open.
Goldman's Q3 earnings growth estimate of 27-28% is the cycle high on the bank's numbers, with growth slowing in each of the next three quarters.

Since the March 2009 lows the S&P is up 16-fold in total return with one recession of about two months, yet U-M consumer sentiment (46.3) is lower than in March 2009 and just printed the second lowest reading on record in data back to 1952.

ZeroHedge's conclusion is that peak earnings, record supply and a depressed consumer make any tactical bounce into the midterms one to sell, while conceding Pasquariello's positioning data is the best argument for the bulls and that rotation into Russell, equal weight and Europe is under way.
